correlations.why: Banks are among the largest companies in the KLCI, so the whole market's mood moves them.
Higher rates usually widen what banks earn on loans over what they pay on deposits (most Malaysian loans are floating-rate).
A weaker ringgit (higher USD/MYR) often comes with foreign investors selling Malaysian assets, banks included.
Higher oil lifts Malaysia's government revenue, exports and the ringgit, which supports the economy and bank lending.
Higher inflation can lead to rate rises (good for margins) but squeezes borrowers (bad for loan quality).
Faster growth means more borrowing and fewer bad loans.
Loan growth is the banks' volume driver.
More bad loans mean higher provisions and lower profit.
More current and savings deposits means cheaper funding and better margins.
Higher yields raise the return on banks' bond holdings over time but cut the value of bonds they already own.
The gap between the average lending rate and the 12-month deposit rate: a wider gap means fatter margins.

drivers.note: Correlation shows how two series moved together in the past, not cause and effect. +1 = always together, -1 = always opposite, 0 = no link.

notes.Base rate: Each bank's reference rate for new floating-rate retail loans (mainly mortgages); it moves with the OPR and the bank's funding cost.
notes.Effective lending rate: Indicative rate a typical new mortgage customer pays (base rate + spread), as published by the bank.
notes.Average lending rate: Average rate on all loans outstanding in the banking system.

niche.note: Niche shares are each bank's group figure as a share of the 9 listed banks combined (from the loan notes in each quarterly report). Market share of system loans uses Malaysian loans only, against Bank Negara's banking-system total.

bank_note: Scores are 0–100 within the 10 banks (higher is better): each metric is ranked, ranks are averaged per category, and the overall score averages the categories. Profit and income figures are the last 12 months to the peer date.

method: Figures are read from each company's own quarterly reports (Group columns), checked so that statements add up, and stored in the Stock Analyst database before any ratio is calculated.
Banks are compared at the latest quarter every bank has reported; non-banks at their own latest quarter, within their subsector.
Industry figures are Bank Negara Malaysia's banking-system statistics.
This page is rebuilt automatically when new quarterly results are processed. It is analysis of reported figures, not investment advice.
